newsitem.title: USA: FAA handling of air traffic control plan criticized.
newsitem.headline: FAA handling of air traffic control plan criticized.

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration failed to provide reliable cost estimates and accounting for the billion-dollar plan to modernize the U.S. air traffic control sytem, a report said on Wednesday.
The General Accounting Office, the watchdog arm of Congress, called the oversight unacceptable in its highly critical evaluation of the FAA's management of the project.

"Without this information, the likelihood of poor investment decisions is increased ... it also means that Congress does not have reliable cost information to use in making funding decisions about FAA," the GAO report said.
"Such a situation is unacceptable when making small investments, but it is especially egregious when making multimillion or billion dollar investments in mission critical systems."

Faced with growing air traffic volume and a deteriorating air traffic control structure, the FAA began in 1981 an ambitious program to update the system that controls the nation's airways. The plan originally was supposed to take about a decade to implement.
The cost of the long-term project, which includes installing both new air traffic control facilities and upgraded computer systems, has been estimated at more than $34 billion between 1982 and 2003.
"Over the past 15 years, FAA's air traffic control modernization projects have experienced substantial cost overruns, lengthy schedule delays and significant performance shortfalls," the GAO said.

The centerpiece of the program -- an advanced automation system -- tripled in cost from $2.5 billion to $7.6 billion and delays in installing it were expected to run eight years or more, according to the report.
The GAO said the agency's cost estimating processes did not satisfy recognized standards and its cost accounting practices did not properly reflect accumulated expenses.

"The result is an absence of reliable project cost and financial information that the Congress has legislatively specified and that leading public and private sector organizations point to as essential to making fully informed investment decisions among competing air traffic control projects," it said.

The GAO recommended that the FAA set up well-defined and officially recognized processes for estimating the cost of projects. It also urged the agency to begin disclosing immediately "the inherent uncertainty and range of imprecision" in all cost estimates presented to Congress.
